text: The structural and thermal analysis task was initiated by first modeling a conceptual design of the conformal tank, to be manufactured and tested in Phase 2. This was to determine the feasibility and capability of the tank to hold 25 kg (or more) of LH2 and to sustain an internal pressure (from LH2) of 13.5 bar and external atmospheric pressure. These are described in sections 2.1 and 2.2 below. Following this, a detailed structural analysis of a cylindrical tank (to be designed and manufactured in Phase 1), was performed. This is described in sections 2.3, 2.4 and 2.5. 2.1. Conformal (Phase 2) tank Outer Shell Buckling Analysis: The outer tank (shell) is meant to protect the inner tank which holds LH2. The primary load on this tank is atmospheric pressure. Hence this tank was analyzed for buckling load under atmospheric pressure. The outer tank was modeled as a sandwich structure with carbon- fiber composite face-sheets sandwiching an Airex foam core. The use of a foam core is a design choice and will be re-visited at the time of detailed design of this tank. A finite element analysis was performed to assess the buckling load of this structure. An initial/notional thickness of 1mm for face-sheets and 5 mm for the foam core, for a total thickness of 7 mm was assumed. For the composite face-sheet, a quasi-isotropic layup of Figure 6: Eigenvalue buckling analysis of outer tank [0/45/-45/90] was assumed. Quasi-isotropic composite s showing first mode (magnified deformation) properties were computed using classical laminate theory (CLT). Ply level material properties were taken from the NIAR NCAMP report [1] for AS4-8552 since material property testing had not yet begun. This material system was deemed to be close enough to the material used to make the tank (IMS65-Q183 resin). Displacement boundary conditions were applied to prevent translation and rotation of the tank. Results: An eigenvalue buckling analysis determined that the first buckling mode has an eigenvalue of 1.96. This is indicative of the margin under atmospheric load. The mode from the first eigenvalue is shown in Figure 6. A second analysis using non-linear FEA (Riks method) was performed and showed that this outer tank can sustain atmospheric pressure- thereby supporting the conclusion of the eigenvalue analysis. Hence, this analysis confirms that the concept is feasible. If there is a need more margin, the face-sheets and/or the foam core can be thickened. During the detailed design phase, the effect of flanges, and boss attachments will be incorporated. Page 7 of 30 Approved for Public Release 2.2. Conformal (Phase 2) tank Inner Tank Internal pressure analysis: A finite element analysis of the conformal inner tank under internal pressure was performed. The inner tank has the same thickness as the over-wrap. Composite material properties used here are the same as in the above tank (AS4-8552). Quasi-isotropic layup [0/45/-45/90]s was assumed. Orthotropic, homogeneous properties of the composite were computed using classical laminate theory (CLT).
